{"id": "54:1/q03", "question": "How near is the Hour, and can its date be calculated?", "turns_on": "Whether nearness is relative admonition or a measurable chronology, and the reliability of chronology reports.", "positions": [{"id": "54:1/q03/p1", "position": "Its time is unknown, but the remaining age is short relative to what has passed.", "reasons": "The Prophet compares his mission and the Hour to adjacent fingers, a day nearly spent, and a depleted pool. {"id": "54:1/q04", "question": "Why is the Resurrection called the Hour?", "turns_on": "The feature of an hour that motivates the name.", "positions": [{"id": "54:1/q04/p1", "position": "Its events or reckoning move swiftly.", "reasons": "al-Māwardī and Bursevī give speed as the naming motive."}, {"id": "54:1/q04/p2", "position": "It comes in the final hour of its day or of the world.", "reasons": "al-Māwardī gives an hour of the Day; Bursevī the world's final hour."}, {"id": "54:1/q04/p3", "position": "A brief interval contains an immense event.", "reasons": "Bursevī explains the time-word by the great event it contains."}]}
{"id": "54:1/q05", "question": "How do the feminine ending and two clauses work?", "turns_on": "Phonology of the feminine suffix and whether conjunction encodes event order.", "positions": [{"id": "54:1/q05/p1", "position": "The feminine tāʾ takes kasra to avoid adjacent sukūns.", "reasons": "al-Naḥḥās attributes this to the Basrans, who treat it as a normally silent particle."}, {"id": "54:1/q05/p2", "position": "The feminine third-person tāʾ is silent because other person forms occupy the available vowels.", "reasons": "al-Naḥḥās attributes the account to Kufans."}, {"id": "54:1/q05/p3", "position": "The moon split first, and the Hour drew near afterward; wāw does not impose temporal order.", "reasons": "Ibn Kaysān and al-Farrāʾ infer an inverted event sequence; Ibn ʿĀshūr says wāw alone does not order the events."}, {"id": "54:1/q05/p4", "position": "The clauses are coordinated, with no change of sense from their order.", "reasons": "al-Naḥḥās calls the second clause coordinated; al-Farrāʾ says reversal does not alter sense."}, {"id": "54:1/q05/p5", "position": "The feminine verbal form itself signals God's great power over the Hour.", "reasons": "al-Biqāʿī reads the form rhetorically."}]}
{"id": "54:1/q06", "question": "Is there a reading with qad before ٱنشَقَّ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "54:1/q06/p1", "position": "Ḥudhayfa reads wa-qad inshaqqa al-qamar, explicitly presenting the split as completed.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya also notes a version without wāw; Ibn Jinnī says qad confirms an anticipated event. al-Ālūsī construes the clause circumstantially."}]}
{"id": "54:1/q07", "question": "What does the verb ٱنشَقَّ describe?", "turns_on": "Whether splitting strictly entails two detached halves.", "positions": [{"id": "54:1/q07/p1", "position": "The moon divided into visible portions.", "reasons": "al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī glosses two segments; Abū Ḥayyān calls it a widening fissure."}, {"id": "54:1/q07/p2", "position": "Strictly, a literal split is a surface fissure; two detached halves are a metonymic extension.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr compares cracks in wood and walls, and treats loss of light as metaphor."}]}
{"id": "54:1/q08", "question": "When and in what sense did the moon split?", "turns_on": "The tense, the sequel in 54:2, report credibility and the nature of the observed phenomenon.", "positions": [{"id": "54:1/q08/p1", "position": "It really split in Muhammad's lifetime, before the Hijra.", "reasons": "Past tense, 54:2, many Companion reports and claimed consensus support it; Zajjāj, Rāzī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Abū Ḥayyān and others reject the future-only reading. Ibn ʿĀshūr accepts the historical miracle while exploring another referent for this verse."}, {"id": "54:1/q08/p2", "position": "It predicts a future split at the Resurrection, with past tense expressing certainty.", "reasons": "Attributed to ʿUthmān ibn ʿAṭāʾ from his father, al-Ḥasan, ʿAṭāʾ and al-Balkhī. al-Ḥasan locates it after the second trumpet. Proponents cite grammatical past-for-future usage and absent global records."}, {"id": "54:1/q08/p3", "position": "The words figuratively mean that a matter became clear.", "reasons": "al-Māwardī cites poetry; al-Qurṭubī invokes a moonlit night; Abū Ḥayyān reports and rejects the extension."}, {"id": "54:1/q08/p4", "position": "The words figure moonrise breaking the darkness, like dawn splitting it.", "reasons": "al-Māwardī and al-Qurṭubī cite al-Nābigha; Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn and Elmalılı reject the analogy."}, {"id": "54:1/q08/p5", "position": "An eclipse or optical effect made observers see two portions.", "reasons": "Asad accepts sincere sighting but suggests partial eclipse; Ibn ʿAbbās reports an eclipse. Fennī allows eye-only miracle; Elmalılı disputes that as deception and says Ibn ʿArabī held an actual split. Doğrul allows eclipse and a symbol of Arab polytheism's doom; al-Ālūsī allows an eclipse alongside a real split."}, {"id": "54:1/q08/p6", "position": "The verse points to a historical split and a further cosmic split near the Hour.", "reasons": "Bursevī allows two times; Elmalılı reads the past miracle as proof of future rupture, and thinks al-Ḥasan and ʿAṭāʾ need not deny it."}]}
{"id": "54:1/q09", "question": "How many times did the moon separate?", "turns_on": "What marratayn counts: events, pieces, or looks.", "positions": [{"id": "54:1/q09/p1", "position": "It split twice.", "reasons": "Anas and others use marratayn; ʿIrāqī claims consensus for two splittings. {"id": "54:1/q14", "question": "Can the physical and scriptural objections to the miracle be answered?", "turns_on": "Whether physical rarity or verses on withheld signs exclude the event.", "positions": [{"id": "54:1/q14/p1", "position": "A real split is possible by God's will; lack of global records or a known mechanism proves no impossibility.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī and Fennī mention clouds, sleep, horizons and inattention; Rāzī invokes Qurʾanic testimony and astrologers' eclipse explanations. al-Ālūsī answers sound, gravity and reunion objections; Elmalılı critiques immutable celestial matter and lists possible mechanisms; Ṭabāṭabāʾī notes brief visibility and absent observatories."}, {"id": "54:1/q14/p2", "position": "A cosmic event should have been universally seen and recorded, and physical rupture and reunion are implausible.", "reasons": "al-Ālūsī reports objections from philosophers and skeptics about records, devastating sound and lost attraction; future-reading advocates cite young transmitters and disputed chains."}, {"id": "54:1/q14/p3", "position": "Qurʾan 17:59 and 17:90–93 indicate requested signs were withheld.", "reasons": "The objection recalls previous peoples destroyed after denying signs. {"id": "55:1/q01", "question": "What does al-Raḥmān mean?", "turns_on": "The notes emphasize respectively the breadth of mercy, its first creative act, or what mercy means when attributed to God.", "positions": [{"id": "55:1/q01/p1", "position": "The One whose mercy is abundant, complete, boundless, and encompasses all beings.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj glosses it as abundant mercy and says earlier scriptures use the name. Ṭabrisī says its mercy encompasses everything; Bursawī distinguishes general worldly provision from forgiveness for believers in the next life, illustrating common bounty with a Persian poem about God's table shared by friend and enemy. Elmalılı says mercy and beneficence are boundless and continuous. Study Quran gives 'Infinitely Good' and 'Loving' as renderings. Al-Biqāʿī says the universal mercy named al-Raḥmān appears through the wonders of creation and its signs."}, {"id": "55:1/q01/p2", "position": "The One whose foundational mercy gives beings existence and their first perfections.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī distinguishes prior mercy in creation from later mercy in provision, understanding, and aid. He reports al-Ghazālī's account of God's care through creation, guidance to faith and happiness, joy in the afterlife, and the vision of His face."}]}
{"id": "55:1/q02", "question": "How does al-Raḥmān relate to al-Raḥīm?", "turns_on": "The distinction is explained either by the sequence and scope of divine acts or by the relation of names to the Essence and acts.", "positions": [{"id": "55:1/q02/p1", "position": "Al-Raḥmān denotes the prior mercy of creation; al-Raḥīm denotes later mercy through sustaining and helping.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says only God creates, whereas people can imitate later mercy by feeding, clothing, and helping.
